title: The reply exp 249 never sent
impact: Moonshot: rejected, and it closes a family. Exp 249 packed a fan-out's stream reruns into one message per reader worker and was rejected because single-write emission latency got 22% (homogeneous) and 66% (heterogeneous) worse; its decision named the cause — a batched reply is indivisible, so the one stream a subscriber is waiting on is delivered only when its two dozen batch-mates finish — and dismissed the fix in one clause: streaming each member back as it finishes 'removes most of the message-amortization the idea rests on'. That clause is checkable now. Exp 284 priced a message to a parked isolate at 0.737 us against 0.445 us to a busy one, exp 136 put the main-isolate completion handler at ~18 us per reply, and exp 283's census found 44% of fan-out reruns and 99.7% of keyed-PK reruns unchanged — and an unchanged member's whole reply is information the main isolate can read from its silence. So the amortization lives in the request send, the worker wake, and the replies that never needed to exist, all of which a streaming-reply batch keeps. Built, and it works: over one 26-burst collection the candidate turned 10,400 rerun request messages into 432 and deleted 7,905 of the replies. Backlog drain, measured on exp 283's sentinel against a zero-ceiling control, moved +2.0% pooled with the sign flipping across the order flip, inside a ±5% floor. A 24:1 cut in messaging is worth nothing, which bounds per-rerun dispatch overhead far more tightly than a counter could and answers exp 283's open question about whether the reader pool is the fan-out constraint. The gate that killed exp 249 also reverses: heterogeneous p50 goes from +66% to −9% to −52% in 4/4 passes, confirming exp 249's own diagnosis of its failure. Tail latency did not resolve and the verdict does not rest on it. Runtime reverted; prototype at `archive/exp-287`. Two protocol hazards recorded for any future multi-reply worker: an unchanged member re-dirtied mid-batch is invisible to invalidation and leaves the stream permanently stale, and re-queueing from inside a partial handler double-dispatches an entry that is both queued and in-flight.
